headline: MLX-VLM v0.4.2 Brings Facebook's Segmentation Model to Apple Silicon
lede: The open-source library mlx-vlm, which lets developers run vision-language models locally on Apple Silicon Macs, released version 0.4.2 with two new model integrations and a round of stability fixes. The headline addition is Meta's SAM 3, a real-time video segmentation model, now usable without cloud infrastructure. A clutch of dtype and processor bugs that had blocked several popular model families were also resolved.
body:
**mlx-vlm** is a Python library built on top of Apple's MLX framework — a NumPy-like array library optimised for M-series chips — that makes it practical to run multimodal AI (models that accept both images and text) on a consumer Mac. The project is maintained by Prince Canuma (GitHub: Blaizzy) and has become a go-to tool for developers who want local inference without renting GPU time.

The most significant new arrival is SAM 3, Meta's third-generation *Segment Anything Model*. Segmentation models don't just classify what's in an image; they draw pixel-precise masks around objects. SAM 3 extends this to video, and the v0.4.2 integration adds real-time label drawing for mask-only output — meaning a developer can feed a live video stream and get animated contours back without a round-trip to a server.

The second new model is **DOTS-MOCR**, an optical character recognition system from rednote-hilab, the AI research arm of Xiaohongshu (the Chinese social platform known in the West as Little Red Book). MOCR is oriented toward multilingual document and scene-text recognition, which fills a gap in mlx-vlm's model roster for non-Latin scripts.

The bug fixes address four model families that had broken or degraded on recent builds. A dtype mismatch in Qwen 3.5's *RMSNorm* layer (a normalization technique that stabilises transformer training) caused silent precision loss; it is now corrected. LFM2-VL, a vision model from Liquid AI, previously required PyTorch to load its processor despite MLX being the inference backend — that dependency is removed. Magistral (Mistral AI's reasoning model) had a flaw in how it counted image tokens before expansion, and PaliGemma (Google's vision-language model) was misrouting keyword arguments to its processor. Both are patched. The fixes matter because each of these models is widely used, and a broken processor quietly produces wrong outputs rather than loud errors.

The release also credits @mdstaff with their first contribution — a patch registering the AutoProcessor hook for Qwen 3.5 — a small marker of a project healthy enough to attract new contributors.

concepts.definition: A neural network that processes both images and text as inputs, enabling tasks like image captioning, visual question-answering, and document OCR. Unlike pure language models, VLMs have an image encoder that translates pixels into a representation the language decoder can reason over.

Apple's open-source array computation framework for Apple Silicon. Unlike PyTorch or JAX, it is designed from the ground up for the unified memory architecture of M-series chips, where CPU and GPU share the same RAM pool, eliminating costly memory copies between devices.

A family of image and video segmentation models from Meta AI. Given a prompt — a point, box, or text label — SAM returns a pixel-level mask isolating the specified object. SAM 3 extends earlier versions with stronger video tracking and real-time performance.

Root Mean Square Layer Normalization, a simplified variant of the standard LayerNorm used in most modern large language models (LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral, etc.). It normalises activations by their RMS rather than their mean and variance, which is cheaper to compute and empirically similar in effect.

The process of extracting machine-readable text from images of documents, signs, or natural scenes. Modern neural OCR models handle distortion, multiple languages, and mixed scripts far better than the rule-based systems they replaced.

repos.summary: mlx-vlm is a Python library for running vision-language models on Apple Silicon via Apple's MLX framework. It wraps model weights from Hugging Face and exposes a unified inference API, a CLI, and a local HTTP server. The project is notable for enabling multimodal AI inference on consumer Mac hardware without PyTorch or GPU rental.
